# Authentication and Connecting to APIs Securely

## Overview
Almost every real API requires you to prove who you are before it will give or accept data, so authentication is a daily part of automation work. The simplest method is an API key - a long secret string you include in your request (often in a header like Authorization or as a query parameter) that identifies your account; anyone with the key can act as you, so it must be kept secret. A Bearer token works similarly, sent in the Authorization header as 'Bearer <token>', and is common with modern APIs. Basic auth sends a username and password encoded in the header, used by older systems. The most important and initially confusing method is OAuth 2.0, which is the technology behind 'Sign in with Google/Facebook' and how Zapier, Make, and n8n connect to your apps: instead of you handing over a password, OAuth redirects you to the app to log in and approve access, then the app gives the automation tool a token to act on your behalf - and you can revoke it anytime. This is why, when you connect Gmail to Zapier, you get a Google login popup. As an engineer you must also respect rate limits (APIs cap how many requests you can make per minute/hour; exceeding them causes errors), and above all you must handle credentials safely: never paste secrets into public places, use the tool's secure credential storage, and rotate keys if leaked. Getting authentication right is the difference between an automation that works reliably and securely and one that breaks or exposes sensitive access.

## Deep Dive
This module covers: API keys and secret tokens; Bearer tokens and Basic auth; OAuth 2.0 flow (the 'Login with...' model); Storing credentials in automation tools; Rate limits and API best practices. Mastering these ideas is essential because they appear repeatedly in production AI systems.

### What You Will Learn
- The core theory behind today's topic.
- How to apply it using Python, NumPy, Pandas, or the relevant framework.
- How to evaluate results and avoid common mistakes.
- Where to find authoritative references when you need deeper detail.

### Real-World Context
In industry, these skills are used daily: data scientists clean messy survey data, AI engineers deploy models to REST APIs, and automation engineers orchestrate pipelines. Today's practical task simulates one of these real-world scenarios.

## Hands-On Practice
Practical Task: Obtain a free API key from a service (e.g., OpenWeather), make an authenticated request including the key in the correct header or parameter, and confirm you get data back; then connect an OAuth app (like Google) inside n8n or Make.
Mini Project: Build an automation that authenticates to two different APIs - one using an API key/token and one using OAuth - fetches data from each, and combines the results, storing all credentials in the tool's secure credential manager.
Assignment: Explain the difference between an API key and OAuth, why OAuth is more secure for connecting third-party apps, and list three rules for handling credentials safely.

Complete all three sections. Each completed section earns points toward your CalibiAI Score. If you are unsure about any part, use the AI assessment popup to submit your work and receive dynamic feedback from DeepSeek.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid
Many beginners rush into coding before fully understanding the data. Others skip validation steps and overestimate model performance. This module helps you build the discipline of checking assumptions first, then applying algorithms systematically.

## Career Impact
The skills covered today are frequently tested in technical interviews and required in entry-level AI engineering roles. Building a portfolio that demonstrates mastery of these concepts will significantly improve your job prospects.

## Key Takeaways
1. Theory guides practice — understand before coding.
2. Clean data and clear metrics are more valuable than complex models.
3. Document your steps for reproducibility.
4. Communication matters: explain results to non-technical stakeholders.
